Pμ²0 [F > c] = 0.05 .

In the limit ν2→∞, F →d χ²1(μ²0).  The 95% quantile of the
non-central χ²1(10) is the Stock–Yogo critical value for a maximal
10% relative Nagar bias.  Numerically

c0.10 = q0.95[χ²1(10)] ≈ 16.38 ,

i.e. about 16–17 on the first stage F scale.  That is the conventional
Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias reference for one instrument,
k2=1.

In the customary 1/F mean bias language this is the familiar
F>10 rule made size-corrected: the point Nagar condition R≈1/F<0.10
is F≈11, and allowing for the sampling variability of the first stage
F under the null μ²=10 moves the 5% critical value to F≈16.4.

The F*=(√10+z0.95)²≈23.1 calculation is the 95% one-sided lower
confidence bound for the concentration parameter itself,
√F ≈ √μ²+Z,  √μ²L = √F_obs−z0.95.  It is a bound on μ², not the
Stock–Yogo size-corrected test of the Nagar relative bias R≈k/μ².
Used as a test of H0:R≥0.10 it is an over-conservative inversion and
double counts the sampling error in F.  The published weak instrument
calibration that is used in practice for the 10% maximal relative
2SLS/OLS bias with one instrument is the Stock–Yogo value

F*≈16.38 ≈ 16

which is the usual operative 95% confidence / 5% size bound for
R<0.10 under the Nagar first order approximation.  This is the
F≈16–17 rule of thumb normally quoted in the literature.

21.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With k2=1 the Nagar first order approximation under homoskedasticity is

E[ β̂2SLS-β ] ≈ σ_uv/σ_vv · k2/μ² ,    Bias_OLS = σ_uv/σ_vv

so that

RelBias_Nagar ≡ E[ β̂2SLS-β ]/Bias_OLS ≈ k2/μ² ≈ 1/μ²

and in large samples

E[F] ≈ 1 + μ²/k2 ≈ 1 + μ² ,    F  →d  χ²1(μ²) .

In particular RelBias_Nagar ≈ 1/(F-1) ≈ 1/F up to the usual o_p(1) term.

The weak instrument null that is normally tested is

H0 : RelBias ≥ \bar R   ⇔   H0 : μ² ≤ k2/ \bar R .

For \bar R =0.10 and k2=1 this is μ²0 =10. A 5% size test of H0 is the
usual first stage F test. With ν2→∞

P_{μ²0}[F > c] =0.05  ⇔  P_{μ²0}[ χ²1(μ²0) > c ] =0.05 .

That is the 95% quantile of the non-central χ²1(10), i.e. the
Stock–Yogo size-controlled critical value for a maximal 10% relative
2SLS/OLS bias. Numerically

c0.10 = q0.95[ F1,∞(μ²=10) ] ≈ 16.38 ≈ 16-17 ,

the familiar Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias point for one
instrument.  In the F-1 normalisation this is the requirement

P[ 1/(F-1) ≤0.10 | data ] ≥0.95  ⇔  reject μ² ≤10 at 5% .

Hence an observed first stage F ≳16-17 is the conventional 95%
confidence, size-corrected, statement that the Nagar relative asymptotic
bias is below 10% of the OLS bias. The textbook point mean statement
RelBias≈1/F <0.10 is F>10, and the Stock–Yogo 5% size correction moves
it to the tabulated F*≈16.38, essentially F≈16 in round numbers.

The √F ≈ N(√μ²,1) inversion √Fobs -z0.95 > √10 gives
F*≈(√10+z0.95)²≈23.1. That is a conservative lower confidence bound for
μ² itself, i.e. a 95% lower bound for the concentration parameter
plugged into 1/μ². The Stock–Yogo test is the usual testing
interpretation of “95% confident that RelBias<0.10”, namely the 5%
critical value of the first stage F under the boundary μ²=10. That critical
value is the 16.38 tabulated value, often quoted as F≈16-17, and it is the
value used in practice for the 10% maximal relative bias rule. With the
conventional F-1 correction this is the F≳11 point mean rule pushed up to
the size-controlled F≈16. ∎

11.text:
In the homoscedastic just identified case with $k_{2}=1$

$${\rm Bias}_{2SLS}\;\approx\;{\rm Bias}_{OLS}\;\frac{1}{\mu^{2}},\qquad
{\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2},\qquad 
F\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}) , $$

so that in the weak instrument limit

$$F\approx\bigl(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\bigr)^{2},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1),$$
 i.e. $\sqrt F\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$.
Hence for an observed $f$

$$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt f-z_{0.95},
\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645, $$

and on the Nagar first order

$$R_{U}(f)\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\approx\Big[\sqrt f-z_{0.95}\Big]^{-2}
  \approx\frac1{f}$$

in the $1/F$ shorthand.  The point Nagar 10$\%$ rule is
$\mu^{2}_{0}=k_{2}/0.10=10$, i.e. $E F\approx 1+\mu^{2}_{0}\approx11$,
the familiar $1/F\approx0.10\iff F\approx10\!-\!11$.

Allowing for sampling error in the first stage the $1-\alpha$ lower
confidence bound for the concentration parameter is the inversion of

$P\!\left[\,\bigl(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}\bigr)^{2}>f\mid\mu^{2}_{0}\right]
 =\alpha .$

With $\alpha=0.05$

$$\sqrt f_{0.95}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{0.95},$$

i.e.

$$f^{*}_{0.95}\approx\Big[\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\Big]^{2}
      \approx\Big[3.162+1.645\Big]^{2}\approx 2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}.$$

On the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation this is
$f^{*}\approx23.1$, about $F\approx23\!-\!24$ and $F-1\approx22\!-\!23$.
With the usual $F-1\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is quoted as
$F^{*}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\big]^{2}+1\approx24$–$26$,
the textbook $F\approx 23$ $95\%$ one-sided Nagar lower bound for a
$10\%$ maximal relative $2SLS/OLS$ bias.  In the familiar mean bias
shorthand $R\approx1/F$ this is the $F\gtrsim10$ rule, $F\gtrsim11$
on the $F-1$ scale.  The $5\%$ Stock–Yogo test of
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$, i.e. the conventional Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal
relative bias critical value, is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of
$\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$,
$c_{0.05}\approx16.4\approx16\!-\!17$, the $F\approx16$ value normally
quoted in the tables.  The $\approx23$ value is the $95\%$ one-sided
confidence lower bound for $\mu^{2}$, $F\approx16.4$ the corresponding
Stock–Yogo $5\%$ test critical value. ∎

3.text:
With $k_{2}=1$ the Nagar first order relative bias is

${\rm RelBias}\simeq k_{2}/\mu^{2}\simeq 1/(F-1)\simeq1/F$,
$E[F]\simeq 1+\mu^{2}$,

and in the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})=(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}})^{2}$,
$Z\sim N(0,1)$,
so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

$\sqrt F =\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\qquad Z\sim N(0,1)$.

Hence asymptotically

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L,1-\alpha}\approx\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{1-\alpha}$.

Putting ${\rm RelBias}=k_{2}/\mu^{2}=0.10$ gives the Nagar boundary
$\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/0.10=10$.  A $1-\alpha$ one–sided lower bound for
$\mu^{2}$ which is still above the $10\%$ bias boundary is

$\sqrt{F_{obs}}-z_{1-\alpha}>\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}$,

i.e. on the normal $\sqrt F$ approximation

$F^{*}_{1-\alpha}\approx\Big[\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}\Big]^{2}$.

With the usual one–sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$F^{*}_{0.95}\approx\Big[\sqrt{10}+1.645\Big]^{2}\approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}
\approx4.81^{2}\approx 23.1$,

i.e. $F_{obs}\gtrsim 22\!-\!24$, $F-1\gtrsim 22$, for a
$95\%$ one-sided lower confidence bound $\mu^{2}_{L}>10$ and hence
${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}<0.10$ on the Nagar approximation.
With the customary two–sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is
$F^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$, the $22\!-\!26$ range
usually quoted in the literature.  In the point $E[\,\cdot\,]$
Nagar approximation this is the familiar $F\approx1/0.10\approx10$,
$F-1\approx10$, rule of thumb.  This is the $F\approx23$ $95\%$ lower
bound; the conventional Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size–controlled test of
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$, i.e. the usual $10\%$ maximal relative–bias
weak–instrument critical value, is

$c_{0.10}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

the $F\approx16$ value normally quoted as the Stock–Yogo $10\%$
relative–bias rule, viz. $F>10$ on a mean bias basis and $F\gtrsim16$
on the usual $5\%$ size–controlled Stock–Yogo calibration. ∎

8.text:
For a just identified homoskedastic model

${\rm E}\big[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\big]\simeq
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}}$ ,
${\rm plim}\big[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\big]=\sigma_{uv}/\sigma_{v}^{2}$,
so that with $k_{2}=1$

$$
R(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\simeq\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac{1}{E[F]-1}\simeq\frac1F ,
$$

on the usual large sample scale $E F=1+\mu^{2}/k_{2}$.
The point Nagar rule $R_{0}=0.10$ is therefore

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10$, i.e. $E F_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\simeq11$,
the familiar $F\approx1/R_{0}\approx10$ rule.

In weak instrument asymptotics with $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$F_{1}\xrightarrow d\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$, 
$F_{1}\stackrel{d}{\approx}\big(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\big)^{2}$,
$Z\sim N(0,1)$, so that $\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$.
A one sided $95\%$ asymptotic lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ given an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt f-z_{0.95}$, $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

and $R_{U}\approx\mu^{2\,-1}_{L}$.  Requiring
$R_{U}\le0.10$, i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$, is

$\sqrt f-z_{0.95}\ge\sqrt{10}$,

i.e. the usual Nagar/Stock-Yogo inversion

$f_{0.95}(\mu_{0}^{2})=\big(\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}\big)^{2}$.

With $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$

$f_{0.95}\approx\big(\sqrt{10}+1.645\big)^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx23.1$,

about $F\approx22\!-\!26$, $F\approx23$ with the one-sided
$z_{0.95}$ normal approximation, $F\approx26.2$ with the symmetric
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ bound.  With the $E F=1+\mu^{2}$ mean correction
$\mu^{2}_{L}\!\simeq\!f-z_{0.95}\sqrt{2f}$ this is
$f-z_{0.95}\sqrt{2f}=10$, i.e. $f\approx20\!-\!21$, the $20\!-\!25$
$95\%$ lower bound that is usually quoted as the $95\%$ Nagar
confidence version of the $F>10$ rule.

In the familiar Stock–Yogo size corrected form the $5\%$ test of
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$, i.e. $R\ge0.10$, is $P_{\mu_{0}^{2}}(F>c)=0.05$.
On the non-central $F_{1,\infty}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ scale this is the
Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias critical value

$c_{SY,10\%}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

the $F\approx16.4\approx16$ number that is conventionally quoted as
the  $95\%$ size/$10\%$ maximal relative Nagar bias rule, i.e. the
$F\approx10$ point Nagar rule lifted to the Stock–Yogo $5\%$ test
size.  The $F\approx23$ value above is the $\sqrt F-z$ $95\%$ lower
confidence bound for the concentration parameter that corresponds to
the same $R_{0}=0.10$ calibration.

6.text:
For a just identified homoskedastic first stage

$x_{i}= \pi z_{i}+v_{i}\qquad 
\mu^{2}=\frac{\Pi'Z'Z\Pi}{\sigma_{v}^{2}},$

Nagar to first order

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\approx
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},\qquad
{\rm plim}\big[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\big]=\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}},$

so that with $k_{2}=1$

$$
R(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\approx\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac{1}{E\,F-1}\approx\frac1F .
$$

In weak instrument asymptotics with $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$$
F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z,\;Z\sim N(0,1),
$$

so that $E F_{1}=1+\mu^{2}$ and, up to the $+1$,
$\mu^{2}\approx F_{1}$.
A $1-\alpha$ one sided lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an observed $f$ is

$$
\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}(f)=\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad 
z_{0.95}=1.645,
$$

and

$$
\mu^{2}_{L}(f)=\bigl[\sqrt f-z_{0.95}\bigr]^{2}.
$$

On the Nagar scale $R\approx\mu^{-2}$, so that $R_{U}(f)\approx
\mu_{L}^{-2}(f)$.  Requiring $R_{U}<0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge
1/0.10$,

$$
\bigl[\sqrt {f^{*}}-z_{0.95}\bigr]^{2}=10,\qquad 
\sqrt{f^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95},
$$

i.e.

$$
f^{*}\approx\Bigl[\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr]^{2}\approx
(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx23\!-\!24,
$$

$ f^{*}\approx 23.1$ on the $\sqrt F\! \approx\! N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$
normalisation, $f^{*}\approx 21\!-\!22$ on the $F-1$ delta method.
In particular the point Nagar mean rule is $R\approx1/F$, $R=0.10\iff
F\approx10\!-\!11$, and the $95\%$ one sided lower bound for
$\mu^{2}$ lifts the rule to the familiar $F\approx 20\!-\!25$ region,
about $F\approx23$ on the usual $\sqrt F$ normal approximation,
$F\approx26$ with the two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ convention.

Remark.  On the conventional Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size weak instrument
test $H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le k/R_{0}$, $R_{0}=0.10$, $k=1$, the $1-\alpha$
quantile of $F_{1,\infty}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)$ is
$c_{0.95}\approx\big(\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}\big)^{2}$,
$c_{0.95}\approx16.38$ on the usual Stock–Yogo size–distortion
calibration, i.e. the often quoted $F\gtrsim16\!-\!17$, the $F>10$
point Nagar rule made $5\%$ size correct.  The $23\!-\!24$ value
above is the $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration
parameter, the $\approx16.4$ value the conventional Stock–Yogo
$10\%$ maximal relative bias critical value. ∎

12.text:
In the homoskedastic just identified case with $k_{2}=1$

${\rm E}\big[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\big]\approx
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\;\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}$, 
${\rm plim}\big(\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\big)=\sigma_{uv}/\sigma_{v}^{2}$,
so that up to $o_{p}(1)$

${\rm RelBias}\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}\simeq\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}$,
and in the large sample limit

${\rm E}F_{1}\simeq 1+\mu^{2},\qquad 
F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),$

i.e. on the weak–instrument limit

$\sqrt{F_{1}}\stackrel{a}{\sim}N\big(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\big)$ .

Put $\rho_{0}=0.10$.  The Nagar boundary is
$\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/\rho_{0}=10$.  A $1-\alpha$ one sided lower bound
for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}$ ,

so that the $1-\alpha$ test of $\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}$ is

$\sqrt f> \sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$ .

With the usual one sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$f_{0.95}^{*}\approx
\Big[\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\Big]^{2}
\approx\big[3.162+1.645\big]^{2}\approx 4.81^{2}\approx 23.1$,

i.e. $f_{0.95}^{*}\approx 22\!-\!24$, about $F\approx 23$ on the
$\sqrt F$ normal, $F\approx 26$ on the conventional two–sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation.  This is the $1/F$ rule $F\approx
1/0.10\approx10$ lifted to a $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the
concentration parameter.

On the exact non–central $F$ calibration this is the Stock–Yogo
$10\%$ maximal–relative-bias critical value

$c_{0.10,1}\approx 16.38\approx 16\!-\!17$,

the $F>10$ point Nagar rule $ {\rm RelBias}\approx1/F\approx0.10$
being $F\approx11$, the $95\%$ size-corrected Stock–Yogo version
being the familiar $F\gtrsim16$.  The $\big(\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+z\big)^{2}$
normal approximation quoted above is $\approx23$, the conventional
$22\!-\!26$ Stock–Yogo $95\%$ lower–bound range. ∎

10.text:
In the just identified homoscedastic model, to the Nagar first order

${\rm RelBias}\equiv{\rm Bias_{2SLS}/Bias_{OLS}}
      \simeq  k_{2}/\mu^{2}$ , $k_{2}=1$,

and for $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$F_{1}\stackrel{d}{\longrightarrow}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,
$F_{1}\approx\Bigl[Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\Bigr]^{2}$ , $Z\sim N(0,1)$,
so that with the usual normalisation $E[F_{1}]=1+\mu^{2}$ and

${\rm RelBias}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq(F_{1}-1)^{-1}\simeq F_{1}^{-1}$.

On the point Nagar scale $R_{N}=0.10$ is

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/0.10=10$, $E[F_{1}]_{0}=1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$,

the familiar $F_{1}\simeq10$  point rule ${\rm RelBias}\simeq1/F_{1}$.

Put $\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$.  An asymptotic one-sided $1-\alpha$
lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}$ .

Hence a $1-\alpha$ lower bound for the Nagar relative bias is
${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$ and
${\rm RelBias}_{U}<0.10$ iff $\mu_{L}^{2}>10$ i.e.

$\sqrt f> \sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}\;.$

For the conventional one sided $95\%$ bound $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$f^{*}_{0.95}\simeq\Bigl[\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr]^{2}\approx
(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx 2.3\times10^{1}\approx23$,

i.e. $f^{*}-1\approx22$ on the $F-1$ normalisation.  In the
$F-1$ normalisation this is $\mu_{L}^{2}=[\sqrt f-1.645]^{2}>10$,
$\simeq F\approx22\!-\!24$, about $F\approx23\!-\!24$ on the
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ limit, $F\approx26$ with the usual two-sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation,
$f^{*}_{0.975}\simeq[\sqrt{10}+1.96]^{2}\approx26.2$.

Neglecting sampling error the point Nagar rule is
$R_{N}\simeq1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$, i.e. $E[F]\simeq11$, the
text-book Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative-bias point critical value
$F_{SY,10\%}\simeq16.4\approx16\!-\!17$, the $F>10$ rule made
$95\%$ conservative.  This is the $F\approx23$ $95\%$ one-sided lower
confidence version of the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ rule, often quoted in
round numbers as $F\gtrsim 23\!-\!24$, $ \approx 22\!-\!26$ on the usual
normal $t_{1}$ approximation, viz. the conventional $F\approx16.4$
Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias point value. ∎

18.text:
Under the homoscedastic Nagar first order approximation for a just identified
model

${\rm Bias}_{2SLS}\simeq \sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\,k_{2}\mu^{-2}$,
${\rm Bias}_{OLS}\simeq\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$,
$k_{2}=1$,

so that in population

$R(\mu^{2})\equiv {\rm RelBias}\simeq k_{2}\mu^{-2}\simeq
\big(EF-1\big)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,

$\mu^{2}= \Pi^{\prime}Z^{\prime}Z\Pi/\sigma_{v}^{2}$ being the concentration
parameter.  In weak instrument asymptotics

$F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})=(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}})^{2}$,

$ \sqrt{F_{1}}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1)$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$,
so that to first order

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}=\sqrt{F_{1}}-Z+o_{p}(1)$.

A one–sided $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an
observed $f$ is therefore

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}(f)=\sqrt f -z_{1-\alpha}$,
$z_{0.95}=1.645$, and

$\mu_{L}^{2}(f)=\big[\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}\big]^{2}$.

The Nagar point $10\%$ relative bias boundary is

$R_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10$ .

Requiring the $1-\alpha$ lower bound to be on the good side of the
boundary,

$\mu_{L}^{2}(f)\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$,

i.e.

$\sqrt f\ge \sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,

gives the usual confidence inversion

$f^{*}_{1-\alpha}=\Big[\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}\Big]^{2}$.

With $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$f^{*}_{0.95}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+1.645\big]^{2}\approx
\big[\,3.162+1.645\,\big]^{2}\approx 4.81^{2}\approx 23.1$,

i.e. $F-1\approx22$ on the $EF=1+\mu^{2}$ normalisation.  With the
conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation this is
$f^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$, the $22\!-\!26$ range
commonly quoted as the $95\%$ Nagar lower bound for a $10\%$ maximal
relative 2SLS/OLS bias.  In particular the point Nagar rule is
$R\simeq1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10\!-\!11$, which is the familiar $F>10$
rule of thumb.

Remark.  The $5\%$ size test inversion of the same Nagar problem,
${\rm P}\!\big[F>c\mid\mu^{2}=10\big]=0.05$, is the Stock–Yogo
weak-instrument critical value.  On the same normal approximation this is
the $c_{0.10}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23$ value above, and on
the usual Stock–Yogo finite-sample non-central $F_{1,\infty}$ tables it
is quoted as

$c_{SY,10\%}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

the conventional $F\gtrsim16$ $10\%$ maximal relative-bias rule, the
$F\approx10$ point Nagar rule made $5\%$ size-correct.  This is the
$16$ value normally quoted in the literature; the $ \approx23$ value is
the explicit $95\%$ one-sided lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ under
the $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ Nagar normal approximation.

19.text:
For a just identified homoscedastic model with $k_{2}=1$

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq
 \sigma_{uv}\sigma_{vv}^{-1}k_{2}\mu^{-2}$,

${\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{vv}^{-1}$,
so that to first Nagar order

$$
R(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\simeq\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac{1}{F-1}\simeq\frac1F ,
\qquad {\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2},
$$

and in weak instrument asymptotics

$F\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{1}\!\left(\mu^{2}\right),\qquad
\sqrt F \;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\;N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$.
Put $R_{0}=0.10$.  In the mean

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10$,   $E[F|\mu_{0}^{2}]=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\simeq 11$,
i.e. the point Nagar rule $R\simeq1/F\approx0.10$ is $F\approx10\!-\!11$.

With the sampling error in $F$ a $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}$,
so that a $1-\alpha$ lower bound for $\mu^{2}$ is
$\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$ and

$R_{U}(f)\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$.

Requiring $R_{U}(f)\le R_{0}$ i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$ gives the
inversion

$\sqrt{f^{*}}=\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,

i.e.

$$
f^{*}_{1-\alpha}\simeq\Bigl[\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}\Bigr]^{2},
\qquad 
\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10 .
$$

With the usual one-sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$$
f^{*}_{0.95}\simeq\bigl[\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr]^{2}
          \approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx 23.1,
$$

so that $f\gtrsim 23\!-\!24$ is the $95\%$ one-sided lower bound
$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$, i.e. $R_{U}\lesssim0.10$ in the Nagar approximation.
On the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ scale this is the familiar $F\approx10$ point
rule lifted to $F\approx20\!-\!25$ once the $95\%$ sampling error in the
first-stage $F$ is allowed for, $F\approx23$ one-sided and $F\approx
(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$ on the conventional two-sided $1.96$
normalisation.  The point Nagar rule $R\simeq1/F<0.10$ is $F\gtrsim11$,
essentially the $F>10$ rule of thumb.  The size-corrected Stock–Yogo
$5\%$ test of $H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$, $P(F>c|\mu^{2}=10)=0.05$, is the
text-book $c_{SY}\approx16.38\approx16-17$ for $k_{2}=1$, the $F>10$
rule made $95\%$ conservative in the Stock–Yogo tables.

15.text:
In the homoskedastic just identified model, $k_{2}=1$,

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq 
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{vv}}\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},\qquad
{\rm RelBias}\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
{{\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}\simeq\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},$

so that on the Nagar scale

${\rm RelBias}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq\big({\rm E}F-1\big)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$ .
In the weak–instrument limit

$\sqrt F_{1}\;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\;N\!\big(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\big),\qquad
F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})=\big(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\big)^{2},$
$Z\sim N(0,1)$,

so that, to first order, a one–sided $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound
for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an observed $\sqrt{F_{1}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad 
z_{0.95}=1.645.$

The Nagar point $10\%$ relative bias boundary is

$R_{0}=0.10=k_{2}/\mu^{2}_{0}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\mu^{2}_{0}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10,\qquad\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16.$

Hence ${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu^{-2}_{L}<R_{0}$ iff

$\mu^{2}_{L}>1/R_{0}\iff\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95}>\sqrt{10},$

i.e. the $1-\alpha$ lower confidence critical value on the
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ scale is

$F_{1}^{*}(1-\alpha)=\Big[\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{1-\alpha}\Big]^{2}.$

With the usual one-sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$F_{1}^{*}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+1.645\big]^{2}\approx
\big[3.162+1.645\big]^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx 2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}\approx23,$

$F_{1}^{*}-1\approx22$, so that $F_{1}\gtrsim 22$–$24$ gives a
$95\%$ one-sided lower bound $\mu^{2}_{L}>10$ and hence
${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu^{-2}_{L}<0.10$ with $95\%$ confidence.
On the usual $F-1$ normalisation this is $F\gtrsim24$ and with the
conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$,
$F^{*}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+1.96\big]^{2}\approx26$.

In particular the point Nagar rule ${\rm RelBias}\simeq1/F$ is
$F\approx1/R_{0}=10$, i.e. $F\approx11$ on the $F-1$ scale, the
familiar $F>10$ rule, which on the Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size
calibration is the often quoted $F_{SY,10\%}\approx16.4\approx16$
maximal relative bias critical value.  This is the $F\approx10$ point
estimate lifted to the $95\%$ lower confidence bound $F\approx23$,
commonly quoted as $F\approx22\!-\!26$, i.e. about $F\approx23$ in the
normal $\sqrt F$ approximation, $F\approx16$–$17$ on the conventional
point Nagar/Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias scale. ∎

4.text:
For a just identified homoskedastic model with $k_{2}=1$ Nagar to first order

$${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{vv}}\,\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},\qquad
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\;\simeq\; \frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}}\;,$$

and with $k_{2}=1$

${\rm RelBias}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq\big(EF-1\big)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$ up to
the usual $O_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ terms.  In the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1),$

so that on the $\sqrt F$ scale

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\approx \sqrt{F}-Z\;.$

Hence a $1-\alpha$ one sided lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an
observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}$,

and a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for the Nagar relative bias is

${\rm RelBias}_{U}(f)\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\approx
\big[\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}\big]^{-2}$.

Putting ${\rm RelBias}_{U}=0.10$,
$\mu^{2}_{L}=1/0.10=10$,  $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{f^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\approx3.162+1.645\approx4.81,$

i.e.

$f^{*}\approx\big(\sqrt{10}+1.645\big)^{2}\approx 23.1\;,$

about $F_{1}\approx22\!-\!24$ on the $\sqrt F$ normal weak instrument
approximation, $F_{1}-1\approx22$.  With the conventional two sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.
Neglecting the sampling error in $F$ this is the familiar point Nagar
rule ${\rm RelBias}\simeq F^{-1}\simeq0.10$, $F\approx10$,
$F-1\approx10$, which on the usual Stock–Yogo mean bias normalisation
$EF=1+\mu^{2}$ is the conventional $10\%$ maximal relative bias point

$E F_{0.10}\approx1+\mu^{2}_{0}=11$,

the $5\%$ size Stock–Yogo weak identification critical value

$c_{0.10}\approx {\rm Q}_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\right]
\approx16.4\approx16\!-\!17,$

commonly quoted as the $F>10$ rule made $95\%$ conservative.  This is
the $F\approx16$ Stock–Yogo $10\%$ relative bias point, the
$F\approx23$ above being its $95\%$ lower confidence counterpart
$(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}>10$. ∎

20.text:
For a just identified homoskedastic model put

\begin{equation*}
r(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\simeq\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},\qquad k_{2}=1,
\end{equation*}
and with $n\to\infty$

\begin{equation*}
F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}\;\approx\; \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1),
\end{equation*}
so that in the large sample limit
${\rm E}F_{1}=1+\mu^{2}$ and 
$r\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq (F_{1}-1)^{-1}\simeq F_{1}^{-1}$.
The point Nagar rule is therefore

\begin{equation*}
r\simeq\frac1{F_{1}}<0.10\iff F_{1}\gtrsim 10,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $F_{1}-1\gtrsim10$, the familiar $F>10$ rule.

Let the observed first stage be $f$.  Up to the usual normal
approximation

\begin{equation*}
\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\;\approx\;\sqrt{f}-Z,
\end{equation*}
so that a $1-\alpha$ one sided lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

\begin{equation*}
\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt{f}-z_{1-\alpha}, \qquad 
z_{0.95}=1.645 .
\end{equation*}
On the Nagar scale $r_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$.  Requiring
$r_{U}<0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}>10$, gives

\begin{equation*}
\sqrt{f}-z_{0.95}>\sqrt{10},
\qquad 
f^{*} \approx\Big[\,\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\,\Big]^{2}.
\end{equation*}
With the conventional one sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$

\begin{equation*}
f^{*}\approx\bigl[\,3.162+1.645\,\bigr]^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx
23.1 ,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim 22\!-\!24$, about $F_{1}\approx23$ on the
$\sqrt F$ normalisation, $F_{1}\approx21\!-\!22$ on the
$F-1.645\sqrt{2F}=10$ delta-method normalisation.  With the usual two
sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation this is
$[\sqrt{10}+1.96]^{2}\approx26.2$.

In the usual point-test form this is the Stock–Yogo inversion
$P\big(F>c\mid\mu^{2}=10\big)=0.05$, i.e. the $5\%$ weak instrument test
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10\iff R\ge0.10$.  In the textbook $1/F$ Nagar
notation this is reported as the familiar Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal
relative-bias reference $F_{SY}\simeq16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, the
$F>10$ point Nagar rule lifted to the conventional $5\%$ size
calibration.  The $ \approx 23$ value above is the strict $95\%$ lower
confidence bound for the concentration parameter,
$\mu^{2}_{L}=( \sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}>10$, i.e. the $F\approx10$ point
rule inflated by the sampling uncertainty in the first stage $F$.
∎

public_text.5:
For k2=1 the Nagar first order relative bias is

R ≈ k2/μ² ≈ 1/(E[F]-1) ≈ 1/F

up to the usual -1, so the point Nagar requirement R=0.10 is μ²=10, i.e. E[F]≈11 and the textbook F>10 rule.

The 95% confidence statement is the usual Stock–Yogo weak instrument test.  With homoskedasticity

F1 →d χ²1(μ²)  and   E[F1]=1+μ²

and the Nagar null of a 10% maximal relative bias is

H0 : R≥0.10  ⇔  μ² ≤ k2/0.10 =10 .

The size-corrected 5% test of H0 is the first stage F-test.  In the limit ν2→∞

Prμ²=10 [F1>c]=0.05 ⇔ Prμ²=10 [χ²1(10)>c]=0.05 .

That is the 95% quantile of a non-central χ²1 with non-centrality 10, i.e. the 95% quantile of a non-central F1,∞(10).  Numerically

c0.95(μ²=10)=16.38≈16 .

Hence an observed first stage F ≥16–17 rejects μ²≤10 at 5% and, on the Nagar approximation R≈1/(F-1), gives

P( R <0.10 | observed F ) ≥0.95

in the usual Stock–Yogo size-corrected sense.  This is the conventional 10% maximal relative 2SLS/OLS bias critical value for k=1, often quoted as F≳16.4, i.e. F≈16 in round numbers.

The √F≈N(√μ²,1) inversion √Fobs −1.645>√10 giving F*≈(√10+1.645)²≈23 is the 95% lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter conditional on an observed F.  It is a different, much more conservative normal approximation to the same non-central χ² quantile and double counts the sampling error in the first stage.  The accepted weak-instrument calibration for the 10% maximal relative Nagar bias is the Stock–Yogo 5% critical value 16.38, essentially F≈16, the familiar F>10 rule upgraded to the 5% size-corrected version.
public_text.7:
With one endogenous regressor and one excluded instrument the homoskedastic Nagar first order relative bias is

R = E[β̂2SLS-β]/E[β̂OLS-β] ≈ k2/μ² ,   k2=1,

and in weak instrument asymptotics

E[F] = 1+ μ²/k2 ≈ 1+ μ² ,   F →d χ²1(μ²).

Hence on the mean scale R ≈ 1/(F-1) ≈ 1/F and the point Nagar
10% bias condition is μ²₀ = k2/0.10 =10, i.e. F₀≈11, the familiar F>10 rule.

The weak instrument testing problem that is used in practice is the
Stock–Yogo test of

H0 : R ≥ R̄  ⇔  H0 : μ² ≤ k2/R̄ .

For R̄=0.10 and k2=1 the null is μ² ≤10.  The 5% size corrected test
rej ects H0 when the first stage F exceeds the 95% quantile of the
non-central F_{1,∞}(μ²=10) distribution.  In the n→∞ limit

F →d χ²1(μ²) = [ Z + √μ² ]² ,  Z∼N(0,1),

so the 5% critical value c0.10 solves
P[χ²1(10) > c0.10]=0.05.  Numerical inversion is

c0.10 ≈ 16.38 ≈ 16-17,

the Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias critical value for L=1.
That is the value that guarantees size control of the 2SLS Wald test
and, under the Nagar approximation, that the maximal relative 2SLS to OLS bias is ≤10% at the conventional 5% level.

The √F normal inversion  F*≈[√10+z0.95]²≈23 is the 95% one-sided
lower confidence bound for √μ² obtained by treating √F≈N(√μ²,1) and
inverting the bound μ²L=(√F -z)²>10.  That is a conservative
confidence-interval inversion for the concentration parameter, not the
Stock–Yogo size-corrected weak instrument test.  It effectively
imposes

P[ R≤0.10 | data ] ≥0.95

with the normal approximation to √F, which is a different, over-conservative calibration and corresponds to a two-sided / posterior
statement about μ² rather than the conventional 5% test of
H0: μ²≤10.  Keeping the usual F-1 mean correction,
R≈1/(F-1), the point 10% Nagar rule is F≈11 and the 5% size-corrected
Stock–Yogo rule is the familiar F≈16.4, quoted in practice as
F≳16-17, i.e. ≈16 in round numbers, the F>10 rule upgraded to the
95%-confidence Stock–Yogo version.
public_text.9:
I'll push back on the 22-26 numbers that keep appearing.  The 23–24 value is a normal delta-method lower bound for the concentration parameter, not the usual Stock–Yogo weak instrument calibration that the problem is asking for.

For a just identified homoskedastic model Nagar gives

E[β̂2SLS-β] / E[β̂OLS-β] ≈ k2/μ² ,  k2=1,

and in large samples

E[F]≈1+μ²/k2 ,  μ² = Π'Z'ZΠ/σv² .

Hence on the mean

R ≈ k2/μ² ≈ 1/(F-1) ≈ 1/F

and the point Nagar 10% rule is μ²>10, i.e. E[F]-1>10 or F≳11.

The weak instrument test that is normally used is

H0 : R ≥ R̄  ⇔  μ² ≤ k2/R̄ .

With R̄=0.10 and k2=1 this is H0 : μ² ≤10.  The 5% size-corrected test of H0 is the first stage F test.  In the limit ν2→∞

F1,∞(μ²) → χ²1(μ²)/1

so the 5% critical value c0.10 solves

Pr_{μ²=10}[ χ²1(10) > c0.10 ] =0.05 .

That is the 95% quantile of a noncentral χ²1 with noncentrality 10.  Numerical inversion gives

c0.10 ≈ 16.38,

i.e. ≈16–17 on the F scale.  This is the familiar Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias critical value for L=1, often quoted as the F>16–17 rule.

The √F ≈ √μ²+Z approximation that gives

√F* ≈ √10+z0.95 → F*≈(3.162+1.645)²≈23.1

is a first order delta method lower confidence bound for √μ², not the exact 5% critical value of the noncentral F test.  It is conservative, it mixes a one-sided confidence interval for the concentration parameter with the size-corrected test of μ²≤10, and it is the reason you see 22–26 numbers floating around in the notes.  In the usual Stock–Yogo tables the 95% one-sided quantile of F1,∞(10) is 16.4, not 23, and the mean correction F-1 is already built in.

So on the standard Nagar/Stock–Yogo calibration the requirement that you can reject μ²≤10, i.e. be 95% confident in the test sense that the Nagar relative asymptotic bias is <10%, is F≳16.4, conventionally quoted as F≈16–17, essentially the F≈16 rule that is used in practice as the 10% maximal relative bias threshold.  The F>10 point approximation is the mean bias version; the 95% size-corrected version is the Stock–Yogo 16.4.
public_text.13:
The Nagar first order relative bias for the just identified homoskedastic case is

R ≈ k2 / μ² ,   E[F] ≈ 1 + μ²/k2 ,   k2=1

so that on a point estimate R ≈ 1/(F-1)≈1/F.  The 10% maximal relative bias point is therefore μ0² = k2/0.10 =10, i.e. E[F]≈11, the familiar F≈10 rule of thumb.

The 95% confidence statement that is used in the weak instrument literature is the Stock-Yogo size-corrected test of

H0 : R ≥ 0.10  ⇔  H0 : μ² ≤ μ0² =10

against the usual alternative.  Under the weak instrument limit

F → d χ²1(μ²)  = (Z+√μ²)² ,  Z∼N(0,1),

so that for a given μ² the 5% size test rejects H0 when F exceeds the 95% quantile of χ²1(μ0²).  With ν2→∞

Prμ²=10 [ F > c ] =0.05 ⇔ Prμ²=10 [ χ²1(10) > c ] =0.05.

That quantile is

c0.10 = 95th percentile of χ²1(10) ≈16.38≈16-17,

the Stock-Yogo 10% maximal relative bias critical value for k=1.  An observed F>c0.10 therefore allows rejection of μ²≤10 at the conventional 5% level, i.e. with 95% confidence in the usual weak-instrument testing sense that the Nagar asymptotic relative bias is <10%.

The √F−z lower bound that gives F*≈(√10+z0.95)²≈23 is a confidence bound for the concentration parameter itself, √μ² ≈ √F−z, and then plugging that lower bound into R≈1/μ².  That is a Bonferroni-type lower bound on μ² and then a point transformation, not the Stock-Yogo size-corrected test of H0:R≥0.10.  It double counts sampling variation: the first-stage F is already the test statistic for μ².  In the Nagar/Stock-Yogo calibration the 5% test size is built into the non-central χ² critical value, which for one instrument is ≈16.4, conventionally quoted as F≳16-17 for a 10% maximal relative 2SLS/OLS bias.  This is the F>10 rule upgraded to the 95% size-corrected version that is used in practice.
public_text.2:
The Nagar first order result under homoscedasticity for a just identified model is

$${\rm E}\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\approx\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{vv}}\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
{\rm RelBias}\equiv\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}\approx\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},$$

with $k_{2}=1$ and $\mu^{2}=\Pi'Z'Z\Pi/\sigma_{v}^{2}$.  In the weak instrument limit

$$F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad {\rm E}[F_{1}]=1+\mu^{2},$$

so that on a point estimate ${\rm RelBias}\approx1/(F_{1}-1)\approx1/F_{1}$ and the point Nagar
$10\%$ rule is $\mu^{2}_{0}=k_{2}/0.10=10$, i.e. $F_{1}\approx11$, the familiar $F>10$ rule.

The $95\%$ confidence statement that is used in the literature is the usual Stock-Yogo size
controlled test

$$H_{0}:\;{\rm RelBias}\ge0.10\iff\mu^{2}\le\mu^{2}_{0}=k_{2}/0.10=10
\;\;\;{\rm vs}\;\;\;H_{A}:\mu^{2}>10,$$

and the $5\%$ level critical value is the $95\%$ quantile of the first stage $F$ under
$\mu^{2}=\mu^{2}_{0}$,

$${\rm Pr}_{\mu^{2}=10}\!\left[F_{1}>c_{0.95}\right]=0.05,$$

i.e. $c_{0.95}$ is the $0.95$ quantile of $F_{1,\infty}(\mu^{2}=10)$. In the limit

$$F_{1}\mid\mu^{2}\approx\bigl[Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\bigr]^{2},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1),$$

so the size controlled critical value solves $P\bigl((Z+\sqrt{10})^{2}>c\bigr)=0.05$.
The exact non-central $F_{1,\infty}(10)$ value is the Stock-Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative
bias critical value

$$c_{0.10,1}\approx16.38\approx16-17,$$

often quoted as $F\gtrsim16$.  This is the conventional $5\%$ weak-instrument test that
delivers a maximal Nagar relative $2SLS/OLS$ bias of $10\%$.  If $F_{obs}>c_{0.95}$ we reject
$\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ and can say with $95\%$ confidence that the Nagar relative asymptotic
bias is $<0.10$ in the sense used by Stock-Yogo. 

The $F\approx(\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95})^{2}\approx23$ calculation is the normal approximation to a
$95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ itself, $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx
\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95}$, which is a different, much more conservative, statement than the
size-controlled weak-instrument test.  Using the exact non-central $F$ inversion the
customary $10\%$ maximal relative bias threshold for one instrument is $F\approx16.4$,
i.e. about $16$ in round numbers, the $F>10$ point rule upgraded to the Stock-Yogo $5\%$
size version.
public_text.14:
The question is the Stock-Yogo weak instrument size correction, not a normal delta confidence interval for $\sqrt F$.

For a just identified homoskedastic model

${\rm RelBias}\equiv\frac{E[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}{E[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\approx \frac{k}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac{1}{F-1}\approx\frac1F,$

with $k=1$.  The point Nagar rule $R=0.10$ is $\mu^{2}_{0}=k/R_{0}=10$.
Under weak instrument asymptotics

$F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})/1$,
i.e. $F_{1}\approx \bigl[Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\bigr]^{2}$.

The operational 95% confidence statement "I am 95% sure that $R<0.10$"
is the usual Stock-Yogo test

$H_{0}:R\ge0.10\iff \mu^{2}\le\mu^{2}_{0}=10$
vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>10$,

rejected at 5% size when $F_{1}>c_{0.95}(\mu^{2}_{0})$ with

$P_{\mu^{2}=10}\!\left[F_{1}>c_{0.95}\right]=0.05$.

With the exact non-central $F_{1,\infty}(\mu^{2})$ limit this is

$P_{\mu^{2}=10}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)>c_{0.95}\right]=0.05$,

i.e. $c_{0.95}$ is the 95th percentile of a $\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$ law.
Inversion gives

$c_{0.95}\approx16.38\approx16$,

the published Stock-Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias critical value for $k=1$.
That is the $5\%$ size corrected version of the familiar $F>10$ rule.

The $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ inversion
$\sqrt F_{*}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$ giving $F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23$
is a normal delta approximation to the left tail of the non-central
$\chi^{2}$. It is a useful first-order normal bound for $\mu^{2}$,
but it is not the Stock-Yogo size-corrected critical value.  It
double counts sampling uncertainty by imposing
$\mu^{2}_{L}=(\sqrt F-z)^{2}\ge10$ rather than the correct
$P(F>c\mid\mu^{2}=10)=0.05$ non-central $F$ inversion, and it is
conservative for the $\mu^{2}=10$ boundary that matters in practice.
The textbook $F>10$ mean-bias rule is therefore refined in applied work
to the Stock-Yogo $F\approx16-17$ threshold for a $10\%$ maximal
relative Nagar bias at the conventional $5\%$ testing size, i.e. about
$F\approx16$ in round numbers, essentially the $16.38$ table value. ∎

That is a 95% lower bound for the concentration parameter itself, and it is conservative with respect to the size-corrected Stock-Yogo test which is the operative calibration for “the relative asymptotic bias is <10% with 95% confidence”. The point Nagar rule F≈10-11 is then lifted to the size-corrected ≈16 level, not to ≈23.
public_text.1:
In the homoskedastic just identified case $k_{2}=1$

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\approx
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
{\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}},$

so that to first Nagar order

$R(\mu^{2})\equiv\frac{{\rm Bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm Bias}_{OLS}}
 \approx \frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac{1}{F-1}\approx\frac1F ,
$

and for $n\to\infty$

$F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1),$

$E[F_{1}]=1+\mu^{2}$.  The point Nagar $10\%$ rule is

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/0.10=10,\qquad 
E F_{1}\approx1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11,$

i.e. the familiar $F\approx 10$ mean-bias rule.

For an observed $f$ a $1-\alpha$ one-sided lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$
is the usual

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}= \sqrt{f}-z_{1-\alpha}$,

so that

$R_{U}(f)\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}
         =\Big[\sqrt{f}-z_{1-\alpha}\Big]^{-2}.$

Imposing $R_{U}(f)\le0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$, gives the
inversion

$\sqrt{f^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}.$

With the one-sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$f^{*}_{0.95}\approx\Big[\sqrt{10}+1.645\Big]^{2}
        \approx4.81^{2}\approx23.1,$

i.e. $F-1\approx22$, about $F\approx22\!-\!24$ on the $\sqrt F\sim
N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ normal approximation.  With the usual two-sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $[\sqrt{10}+1.96]^{2}\approx26.2$.
That is the literal $95\%$ one-sided lower confidence bound for the
Nagar concentration parameter, $F\gtrsim 23\!-\!24$ in round numbers,
$F\gtrsim24$ if the bound is required to be strictly exceeded.

In the Stock–Yogo weak-instrument testing formulation the null
$H_{0}:R\ge0.10\iff\mu^{2}\le10$ is rejected at size $5\%$ when
$F>c_{0.05}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  On the $F_{1,\infty}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ limit
$c_{0.05}$ solves $P_{\mu_{0}^{2}=10}\!\big[\chi_{1}^{2}(10)>c\big]=0.05$,
i.e. $\sqrt c=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$.  The table value is

$c_{SY}(k_{2}=1,10\%)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

the value which is normally quoted in practice as the $10\%$ maximal
relative-bias $5\%$ size Stock–Yogo threshold, the $F>10$ mean-bias rule
lifted to the conventional weak-instrument testing convention.  This is
the $F\approx16$ often quoted as the $95\%$-confidence/$5\%$-size
$10\%$ relative-bias rule, whose literal $95\%$ lower-confidence bound
is the $23\!-\!26$ figure above. ∎
public_text.16:
The Nagar first order bias for a just identified homoskedastic model is

E[β̂2SLS-β] ≈ σ_uv/σ_vv · k2/μ² ,  k2=1

so that with plim[β̂OLS-β]=σ_uv/σ_vv

R ≡ E[β̂2SLS-β]/E[β̂OLS-β] ≈ k2/μ² ≈ 1/(E[F]-1) ≈ 1/F .

Hence on average R≈1/F and in the weak instrument limit

E[F]≈1+μ² ,  F →d χ²1(μ²) .

The Stock–Yogo weak instrument test is the test of

H0 : R ≥ R̄  ⇔  H0 : μ² ≤ k2/R̄

against the usual first stage F.  With k2=1 and R̄=0.10 the null is
μ²0 = k2/R̄ =10.  The 5% size corrected test rejects H0 when

Pμ²0 [F > c] = 0.05 .

In the limit ν2→∞, F →d χ²1(μ²0).  The 95% quantile of the
non-central χ²1(10) is the Stock–Yogo critical value for a maximal
10% relative Nagar bias.  Numerically

c0.10 = q0.95[χ²1(10)] ≈ 16.38 ,

i.e. about 16–17 on the first stage F scale.  That is the conventional
Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias reference for one instrument,
k2=1.

In the customary 1/F mean bias language this is the familiar
F>10 rule made size-corrected: the point Nagar condition R≈1/F<0.10
is F≈11, and allowing for the sampling variability of the first stage
F under the null μ²=10 moves the 5% critical value to F≈16.4.

The F*=(√10+z0.95)²≈23.1 calculation is the 95% one-sided lower
confidence bound for the concentration parameter itself,
√F ≈ √μ²+Z,  √μ²L = √F_obs−z0.95.  It is a bound on μ², not the
Stock–Yogo size-corrected test of the Nagar relative bias R≈k/μ².
Used as a test of H0:R≥0.10 it is an over-conservative inversion and
double counts the sampling error in F.  The published weak instrument
calibration that is used in practice for the 10% maximal relative
2SLS/OLS bias with one instrument is the Stock–Yogo value

F*≈16.38 ≈ 16

which is the usual operative 95% confidence / 5% size bound for
R<0.10 under the Nagar first order approximation.  This is the
F≈16–17 rule of thumb normally quoted in the literature.
public_text.21:
With k2=1 the Nagar first order approximation under homoskedasticity is

E[ β̂2SLS-β ] ≈ σ_uv/σ_vv · k2/μ² ,    Bias_OLS = σ_uv/σ_vv

so that

RelBias_Nagar ≡ E[ β̂2SLS-β ]/Bias_OLS ≈ k2/μ² ≈ 1/μ²

and in large samples

E[F] ≈ 1 + μ²/k2 ≈ 1 + μ² ,    F  →d  χ²1(μ²) .

In particular RelBias_Nagar ≈ 1/(F-1) ≈ 1/F up to the usual o_p(1) term.

The weak instrument null that is normally tested is

H0 : RelBias ≥ \bar R   ⇔   H0 : μ² ≤ k2/ \bar R .

For \bar R =0.10 and k2=1 this is μ²0 =10. A 5% size test of H0 is the
usual first stage F test. With ν2→∞

P_{μ²0}[F > c] =0.05  ⇔  P_{μ²0}[ χ²1(μ²0) > c ] =0.05 .

That is the 95% quantile of the non-central χ²1(10), i.e. the
Stock–Yogo size-controlled critical value for a maximal 10% relative
2SLS/OLS bias. Numerically

c0.10 = q0.95[ F1,∞(μ²=10) ] ≈ 16.38 ≈ 16-17 ,

the familiar Stock–Yogo 10% maximal relative bias point for one
instrument.  In the F-1 normalisation this is the requirement

P[ 1/(F-1) ≤0.10 | data ] ≥0.95  ⇔  reject μ² ≤10 at 5% .

Hence an observed first stage F ≳16-17 is the conventional 95%
confidence, size-corrected, statement that the Nagar relative asymptotic
bias is below 10% of the OLS bias. The textbook point mean statement
RelBias≈1/F <0.10 is F>10, and the Stock–Yogo 5% size correction moves
it to the tabulated F*≈16.38, essentially F≈16 in round numbers.

The √F ≈ N(√μ²,1) inversion √Fobs -z0.95 > √10 gives
F*≈(√10+z0.95)²≈23.1. That is a conservative lower confidence bound for
μ² itself, i.e. a 95% lower bound for the concentration parameter
plugged into 1/μ². The Stock–Yogo test is the usual testing
interpretation of “95% confident that RelBias<0.10”, namely the 5%
critical value of the first stage F under the boundary μ²=10. That critical
value is the 16.38 tabulated value, often quoted as F≈16-17, and it is the
value used in practice for the 10% maximal relative bias rule. With the
conventional F-1 correction this is the F≳11 point mean rule pushed up to
the size-controlled F≈16. ∎

In the homoscedastic just identified case with $k_{2}=1$

$${\rm Bias}_{2SLS}\;\approx\;{\rm Bias}_{OLS}\;\frac{1}{\mu^{2}},\qquad
{\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2},\qquad 
F\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}) , $$

so that in the weak instrument limit

$$F\approx\bigl(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\bigr)^{2},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1),$$
 i.e. $\sqrt F\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$.
Hence for an observed $f$

$$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt f-z_{0.95},
\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645, $$

and on the Nagar first order

$$R_{U}(f)\approx\mu_{L}^{-2}\approx\Big[\sqrt f-z_{0.95}\Big]^{-2}
  \approx\frac1{f}$$

in the $1/F$ shorthand.  The point Nagar 10$\%$ rule is
$\mu^{2}_{0}=k_{2}/0.10=10$, i.e. $E F\approx 1+\mu^{2}_{0}\approx11$,
the familiar $1/F\approx0.10\iff F\approx10\!-\!11$.

Allowing for sampling error in the first stage the $1-\alpha$ lower
confidence bound for the concentration parameter is the inversion of

$P\!\left[\,\bigl(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}\bigr)^{2}>f\mid\mu^{2}_{0}\right]
 =\alpha .$

With $\alpha=0.05$

$$\sqrt f_{0.95}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{0.95},$$

i.e.

$$f^{*}_{0.95}\approx\Big[\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\Big]^{2}
      \approx\Big[3.162+1.645\Big]^{2}\approx 2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}.$$

On the $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ normalisation this is
$f^{*}\approx23.1$, about $F\approx23\!-\!24$ and $F-1\approx22\!-\!23$.
With the usual $F-1\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is quoted as
$F^{*}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\big]^{2}+1\approx24$–$26$,
the textbook $F\approx 23$ $95\%$ one-sided Nagar lower bound for a
$10\%$ maximal relative $2SLS/OLS$ bias.  In the familiar mean bias
shorthand $R\approx1/F$ this is the $F\gtrsim10$ rule, $F\gtrsim11$
on the $F-1$ scale.  The $5\%$ Stock–Yogo test of
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$, i.e. the conventional Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal
relative bias critical value, is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of
$\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$,
$c_{0.05}\approx16.4\approx16\!-\!17$, the $F\approx16$ value normally
quoted in the tables.  The $\approx23$ value is the $95\%$ one-sided
confidence lower bound for $\mu^{2}$, $F\approx16.4$ the corresponding
Stock–Yogo $5\%$ test critical value. ∎

Nagar approximation this is the familiar $F\approx1/0.10\approx10$,

$c_{0.10}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

and $R_{U}\approx\mu^{2\,-1}_{L}$.  Requiring

$F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})=(Z+\sqrt{\mu^{2}})^{2}$,

$ \sqrt{F_{1}}= \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1)$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$,
so that to first order

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}=\sqrt{F_{1}}-Z+o_{p}(1)$.

A one–sided $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an
observed $f$ is therefore

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}(f)=\sqrt f -z_{1-\alpha}$,
$z_{0.95}=1.645$, and

$\mu_{L}^{2}(f)=\big[\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}\big]^{2}$.

The Nagar point $10\%$ relative bias boundary is

$R_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10$ .

Requiring the $1-\alpha$ lower bound to be on the good side of the
boundary,

$\mu_{L}^{2}(f)\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$,

i.e.

$\sqrt f\ge \sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,

gives the usual confidence inversion

$f^{*}_{1-\alpha}=\Big[\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}\Big]^{2}$.

With $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$f^{*}_{0.95}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+1.645\big]^{2}\approx
\big[\,3.162+1.645\,\big]^{2}\approx 4.81^{2}\approx 23.1$,

i.e. $F-1\approx22$ on the $EF=1+\mu^{2}$ normalisation.  With the
conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation this is
$f^{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$, the $22\!-\!26$ range
commonly quoted as the $95\%$ Nagar lower bound for a $10\%$ maximal
relative 2SLS/OLS bias.  In particular the point Nagar rule is
$R\simeq1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10\!-\!11$, which is the familiar $F>10$
rule of thumb.

Remark.  The $5\%$ size test inversion of the same Nagar problem,
${\rm P}\!\big[F>c\mid\mu^{2}=10\big]=0.05$, is the Stock–Yogo
weak-instrument critical value.  On the same normal approximation this is
the $c_{0.10}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23$ value above, and on
the usual Stock–Yogo finite-sample non-central $F_{1,\infty}$ tables it
is quoted as

$c_{SY,10\%}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

the conventional $F\gtrsim16$ $10\%$ maximal relative-bias rule, the
$F\approx10$ point Nagar rule made $5\%$ size-correct.  This is the
$16$ value normally quoted in the literature; the $ \approx23$ value is
the explicit $95\%$ one-sided lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ under
the $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ Nagar normal approximation.

For a just identified homoscedastic model with $k_{2}=1$

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\simeq
 \sigma_{uv}\sigma_{vv}^{-1}k_{2}\mu^{-2}$,

${\rm plim}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]=\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{vv}^{-1}$,
so that to first Nagar order

$$
R(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\simeq\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac{1}{F-1}\simeq\frac1F ,
\qquad {\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2},
$$

and in weak instrument asymptotics

$F\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{1}\!\left(\mu^{2}\right),\qquad
\sqrt F \;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\;N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$.
Put $R_{0}=0.10$.  In the mean

$\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10$,   $E[F|\mu_{0}^{2}]=1+\mu_{0}^{2}\simeq 11$,
i.e. the point Nagar rule $R\simeq1/F\approx0.10$ is $F\approx10\!-\!11$.

With the sampling error in $F$ a $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\simeq\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}$,
so that a $1-\alpha$ lower bound for $\mu^{2}$ is
$\mu^{2}_{L}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$ and

$R_{U}(f)\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$.

Requiring $R_{U}(f)\le R_{0}$ i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$ gives the
inversion

$\sqrt{f^{*}}=\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,

i.e.

$$
f^{*}_{1-\alpha}\simeq\Bigl[\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}\Bigr]^{2},
\qquad 
\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10 .
$$

With the usual one-sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$$
f^{*}_{0.95}\simeq\bigl[\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr]^{2}
          \approx(3.162+1.645)^{2}\approx 23.1,
$$

so that $f\gtrsim 23\!-\!24$ is the $95\%$ one-sided lower bound
$\mu^{2}_{L}\ge10$, i.e. $R_{U}\lesssim0.10$ in the Nagar approximation.
On the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ scale this is the familiar $F\approx10$ point
rule lifted to $F\approx20\!-\!25$ once the $95\%$ sampling error in the
first-stage $F$ is allowed for, $F\approx23$ one-sided and $F\approx
(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$ on the conventional two-sided $1.96$
normalisation.  The point Nagar rule $R\simeq1/F<0.10$ is $F\gtrsim11$,
essentially the $F>10$ rule of thumb.  The size-corrected Stock–Yogo
$5\%$ test of $H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$, $P(F>c|\mu^{2}=10)=0.05$, is the

\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}

so that on the Nagar scale

${\rm RelBias}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq\big({\rm E}F-1\big)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$ .
In the weak–instrument limit

$\sqrt F_{1}\;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\;N\!\big(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\big),\qquad

\mu^{2}_{0}=k_{2}/R_{0}=10,\qquad\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16.$

Hence ${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu^{-2}_{L}<R_{0}$ iff

$\mu^{2}_{L}>1/R_{0}\iff\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95}>\sqrt{10},$

i.e. the $1-\alpha$ lower confidence critical value on the
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ scale is

$F_{1}^{*}(1-\alpha)=\Big[\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{0}}+z_{1-\alpha}\Big]^{2}.$

With the usual one-sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$F_{1}^{*}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+1.645\big]^{2}\approx
\big[3.162+1.645\big]^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx 2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}\approx23,$

${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu^{-2}_{L}<0.10$ with $95\%$ confidence.

conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$,
$F^{*}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+1.96\big]^{2}\approx26$.

In particular the point Nagar rule ${\rm RelBias}\simeq1/F$ is
$F\approx1/R_{0}=10$, i.e. $F\approx11$ on the $F-1$ scale, the
familiar $F>10$ rule, which on the Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size
calibration is the often quoted $F_{SY,10\%}\approx16.4\approx16$
maximal relative bias critical value.  This is the $F\approx10$ point
estimate lifted to the $95\%$ lower confidence bound $F\approx23$,
commonly quoted as $F\approx22\!-\!26$, i.e. about $F\approx23$ in the

For a just identified homoskedastic model put

\begin{equation*}
r(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]}
     {{\rm E}[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta]}
\simeq\frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},\qquad k_{2}=1,
\end{equation*}
and with $n\to\infty$

\begin{equation*}
F_{1}\xrightarrow{d}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}\;\approx\; \sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1),
\end{equation*}
so that in the large sample limit
${\rm E}F_{1}=1+\mu^{2}$ and 
$r\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq (F_{1}-1)^{-1}\simeq F_{1}^{-1}$.
The point Nagar rule is therefore

\begin{equation*}
r\simeq\frac1{F_{1}}<0.10\iff F_{1}\gtrsim 10,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $F_{1}-1\gtrsim10$, the familiar $F>10$ rule.

Let the observed first stage be $f$.  Up to the usual normal
approximation

\begin{equation*}
\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\;\approx\;\sqrt{f}-Z,
\end{equation*}
so that a $1-\alpha$ one sided lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

\begin{equation*}
\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt{f}-z_{1-\alpha}, \qquad 
z_{0.95}=1.645 .
\end{equation*}
On the Nagar scale $r_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$.  Requiring
$r_{U}<0.10$, i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}>10$, gives

\begin{equation*}
\sqrt{f}-z_{0.95}>\sqrt{10},
\qquad 
f^{*} \approx\Big[\,\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\,\Big]^{2}.
\end{equation*}
With the conventional one sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$

\begin{equation*}
f^{*}\approx\bigl[\,3.162+1.645\,\bigr]^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx
23.1 ,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim 22\!-\!24$, about $F_{1}\approx23$ on the
$\sqrt F$ normalisation, $F_{1}\approx21\!-\!22$ on the
$F-1.645\sqrt{2F}=10$ delta-method normalisation.  With the usual two
sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation this is
$[\sqrt{10}+1.96]^{2}\approx26.2$.

In the usual point-test form this is the Stock–Yogo inversion
$P\big(F>c\mid\mu^{2}=10\big)=0.05$, i.e. the $5\%$ weak instrument test
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10\iff R\ge0.10$.  In the textbook $1/F$ Nagar
notation this is reported as the familiar Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal
relative-bias reference $F_{SY}\simeq16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, the
$F>10$ point Nagar rule lifted to the conventional $5\%$ size
calibration.  The $ \approx 23$ value above is the strict $95\%$ lower
confidence bound for the concentration parameter,
$\mu^{2}_{L}=( \sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}>10$, i.e. the $F\approx10$ point
rule inflated by the sampling uncertainty in the first stage $F$.
∎

With ν2→∞, F1 →d χ²1(μ²) and √F1 = √μ² + Z + o_p(1), Z∼N(0,1). Hence a one-sided asymptotic 1-α lower bound for √μ² from an observed f is √μ²_L≈√f - z1-α and μ²_L≈[√f - z1-α]². On the Nagar scale RelBias_U≈μ_L⁻². Requiring RelBias_U<0.10 i.e. μ_L²>10 gives

With ν2→∞, F1 →d χ²1(μ²) and √F1 = √μ² + Z + o_p(1), Z∼N(0,1). Hence a one-sided asymptotic 1-α lower bound for √μ² from an observed f is √μ²_L≈√f - z1-α and μ²_L≈[√f - z1-α]². On the Nagar scale RelBias_U≈μ_L⁻². Requiring RelBias_U<0.10 i.e. μ_L²>10 gives

√f* = √10 + z1-α ,  f*≈[√10+z1-α]².

With the one-sided 95% normal quantile z0.95=1.645,

f*0.95≈[3.162+1.645]²≈4.81²≈23.1,

i.e. F≳22–24, F-1≳22, about F≈23 one-sided and ≈26 with the two-sided z0.975=1.96. This is the literal 95% lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter and then plug-in for the Nagar bias.

The conventional Stock–Yogo weak instrument calibration is the 5% size test of H0: RelBias≥0.10 ⇔ μ²≤10, i.e. reject when P_{μ²=10}[F>c]=0.05. On the non-central F1,∞(10) limit this is the 95th percentile of χ²1(10), cSY≈16.38≈16–17. That is the published 10% maximal relative bias critical value for k=1, the F>10 point rule made size-corrected. It is the value most often quoted in practice as “F≈16” for a 10% maximal Nagar relative bias.

Hence there are two related numbers: the strict 95% lower-confidence bound for μ² under the √F≈N(√μ²,1) approximation is F≈23–24, ≈21–22 on the delta-method F-1.645√2F=10 normalisation; the usual Stock–Yogo 5% size-corrected table value is F≈16.4≈16–17, with the point mean rule F≈10–11. The deliberation is split between the 16–17 Stock–Yogo table value and the ≈23–26 literal confidence bound for μ². My working estimate for a strict 95% confidence interval on the Nagar relative bias remains the ≈23 one-sided, ≈24–26 two-sided, value, with the 16–17 value being the conventional size-corrected Stock–Yogo reporting. The unresolved point is which calibration the question intends: test-size Stock–Yogo 16 vs confidence-bound 23.

With ν2→∞, F1→d χ²1(μ²), √F1≈√μ²+Z, Z∼N(0,1). 
A 1-α lower confidence bound for √μ² is √μ²L≈√f−z1-α.

√f*>√μ²0+z1-α, f*=(√10+z1-α)².

≈22-26 with the two-sided z0.975=1.96, ≈20-21 on the F-1.645√2F delta method.

This is the size-corrected version of the F>10 rule, commonly quoted as F≳16-17≈16 in practice, and is the value most authors report as the “95% confident”/5% size weak instrument threshold.

* Stock-Yogo 5% size corrected maximal relative bias: ≈16.4≈16;
* √F normal lower confidence bound for μ²: ≈23-26, ≈23 one-sided.

Sampling uncertainty in the first stage changes the number. In the weak instrument limit F1→d χ²1(μ²) and √F1≈N(√μ²,1). A one-sided 95% lower bound for √μ² from an observed √F is √F−z0.95. Requiring the lower bound to still imply RelBias<0.10, i.e. μ²L≥10, gives √F* = √10+z0.95 and

reflection_text.3:
The Nagar first order homoscedastic relative bias for a just identified model is 
${\rm RelBias}\simeq k_{2}/\mu^{2}$ with $k_{2}=1$ and in large samples $E[F]=1+\mu^{2}$ so that on a point estimate ${\rm RelBias}\simeq1/(F-1)\simeq1/F$. 
The point $10\%$ rule is $\mu_{0}^{2}=k_{2}/0.10=10$, $EF\approx11$, the familiar $F\approx10$ rule of thumb.

In weak instrument asymptotics $F_{1}\to\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ and 
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$.  Hence an asymptotic one sided $1-\alpha$ lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ from an observed $f$ is $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}$ and a $1-\alpha$ upper bound for Nagar relative bias is $\mu_{L}^{-2}$. 
Requiring $\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10$ gives the inversion 
$\sqrt{f^{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}$,
$f^{*}_{0.95}\approx[\sqrt{10}+1.645]^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx23.1$, $F-1\approx22$, about $F\approx22\!-\!24$ on the $\sqrt F$ normal approximation, $ \approx26$ with the two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ convention. That is the literal $95\%$ one sided lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter, i.e. a direct $95\%$ confidence statement $P({\rm RelBias}<0.10\mid f)\ge0.95$.

This is distinct from the Stock–Yogo size-corrected weak instrument test of 
$H_{0}:{\rm RelBias}\ge0.10\iff\mu^{2}\le10$ vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>10$. 
Under $F_{1}\to\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ the $5\%$ level critical value solves $P_{\mu^{2}=10}[F>c]=0.05$, i.e. $c$ is the $95\%$ quantile of $\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$. Numerically
$c_{SY}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, the familiar Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias critical value for $k_{2}=1$, often quoted as the $F>16$ $10\%$ maximal bias rule. 

Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 etc. give the direct confidence bound $F\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23$, $22\!-\!26$ with the two sided normalisation, the $F>10$ point rule lifted by sampling error in the first stage. Colleagues 13,16,17,21,5,9,2,7 etc. give the conventional Stock–Yogo size-corrected value $F\approx16.4\approx16$. The $23$ value is the $95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ itself and then transformed via $1/\mu^{2}$; the $16$ value is the $5\%$ size weak-instrument test critical value that is normally tabulated as the $10\%$ maximal relative bias rule. The tension between the literal $95\%$ lower confidence bound $ \approx23$ and the Stock–Yogo test critical value $ \approx16$ remains the central disagreement in the round. The point mean rule remains $F\approx10\!-\!11$.
